newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl won't rule out cabinet reshuffle before poll.
newsitem.headline: Kohl won't rule out cabinet reshuffle before poll.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Thursday he saw no need for a cabinet reshuffle at the moment, but did not rule out the possiblity before September 1998 general elections.
"I have no reason to be dissatisfied with my cabinet colleagues," Kohl told ZDF television in the transcript of an interview recorded at his holiday home in Austria.
"We're talking here about topical political matters and for me at this moment there is no cabinet reshuffle," Kohl said in the interview, which is due to be broadcast on Sunday.

Asked whether "at this moment" meant he was ruling out a reshuffle for this year and next, Kohl replied: "There I am still completely open. But I don't want to expound now on what I am going to do before the election."
Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday repeated a call for a cabinet reshuffle soon, saying a shake-up would make Kohl's 17-member cabinet more effective in the run-up to the election.

"The chancellor has the right a year before the elections to put together a team with which he would want to rule for four years," Waigel told the Bild daily. "I would expect the coalition to gain extra momentum."
Kohl's cabinet contains politicians from his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and its sister party, Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), as well as liberal Free Democrats (FDP).
Commentators have said a shake-up is overdue and could reverse the government's steep slide in opinion polls.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a CSU member, said Kohl should act like a soccer coach and make a few substitutions.
"We are now in the last 20 minutes of the game. We have a new, difficult away game in front of us -- the parliamentary elections," Stoiber told Sat1 television.

Although Kohl made numerous major changes in his cabinet in his first three terms, there has only been one minor change in the first three years of his fourth term -- the FDP justice minister resigned and was replaced by another FDP politician.

Commentators consider Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt (FDP), Interior Minister Manfred Kanther (CDU), Labour Minister Norbert Bluem (CDU) and Family Minister Claudia Nolte (CDU) among those most likely to be dropped in any reshuffle.
Kohl said Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch (CSU) would leave his job this autumn as planned when his ministry is wound up.
This would change the balance of the parties in the coalition, Kohl said, adding this would have to be discussed with the CSU.
Waigel, the CSU leader, has had his reputation dented by numerous setbacks in his efforts to qualify for Europe's single currency and pass key tax reforms.

When the going has got tough in the past, speculation has mounted that he might take over the foreign affairs portfolio, passing the job of finance minister to the FDP in the coalition, who are explicitly committed to tax cuts.
But Waigel told Bild he was not seeking to grab Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel's job.

"Honestly. I wasn't thinking about myself at all. I enjoy my job," Waigel said. "I'm talking about something else. It is already clear that one or two ministers...in the government want to quit after the next general election.
"It is legitimate to say: Let's bring forward these changes -- which would be necessary anyway after the elections -- to help the coalition."
